summary: A Mole leaves his spring cleaning, meets a river for the first time and befriends the Water Rat. Together they row, picnic and visit the vain, car-mad Toad, whose passions end with him in prison. The animals face the Wild Wood, where Badger lives, and an odd night search for Otter's lost son brings them close to the god Pan. In the last chapters Toad escapes disguised as a washerwoman, and his friends retake Toad Hall from the stoats and weasels who have moved in.
context: Kenneth Grahame published the book in 1908 with Methuen in Britain and Scribner in the United States. It grew from bedtime stories and letters about a toad that he sent to his young son Alastair, who was born in 1900. Grahame retired from the Bank of England in 1908 and moved to Blewbury in Berkshire. Theodore Roosevelt wrote to him about the book in 1909. By 1951 it had reached 100 editions in Britain. E. H. Shepard illustrated it in 1931.

people.note: A river dweller who takes Mole in and later helps rescue Toad.

people.name: Toad

people.note: A fearless fighter who helps clear the Wild-Wooders from Toad Hall.

Pink Floyd name an album after chapter 7, The Piper at the Gates of Dawn.

ideas.title: Home against the wild
ideas.note: The cosy river bank is set against the dangerous Wild Wood, with Toad Hall in between as the home to win back.

ideas.title: Friendship and loyalty
ideas.note: Rat, Mole and Badger keep rescuing a boastful friend and help him recover his house.

ideas.title: A god among the reeds
ideas.note: Chapter 7 gives Pan a single quiet appearance, apart from the comic Toad plot.

ideas.title: Stories that began aloud
ideas.note: The book grew out of bedtime tales and letters to a child.

passages.quote: The Mole was bewitched, entranced, fascinated.
passages.why: Mole's first reaction to the river, near the opening of the book.

passages.quote: “And beyond the Wild Wood again?” he asked; “where it’s all blue and dim, and one sees what may be hills or perhaps they mayn’t, and something like the smoke of towns, or is it only cloud-drift?” “Beyond the Wild Wood comes the Wide World,” said the Rat.
passages.why: Rat describes the world beyond the Wild Wood to a curious Mole.

passages.quote: Little Portly is missing again; and you know what a lot his father thinks of him, though he never says much about it.” “What, that child?” said the Mole lightly.
passages.why: The worry that sends Rat and Mole out on the night of the Pan chapter.

passages.quote: Now the gaoler had a daughter, a pleasant wench and good-hearted, who assisted her father in the lighter duties of his post.
passages.why: The gaoler's daughter enters Toad's prison story in chapter VIII.

passages.quote: What haven’t I heard?” “Do you mean to tell me,” shouted the Rat, thumping with his little fist upon the table, “that you’ve heard nothing about the Stoats and Weasels?” “What, the Wild Wooders?” cried Toad, trembling in every limb.
passages.why: News of the Wild Wooders who have taken over Toad Hall.
